title: Pulmonary tumor embolism: A retrospective study over a 30-year period

content: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a common form of venous thromboembolism (VTE), most commonly originating from the lower extremity proximal veins as a deep venous thrombosis (DVT). PE spans a broad spectrum of presentations, ranging from asymptomatic and incidentally discovered to rapidly fatal. An estimated 100,000-180,000 annual deaths result from PE in the United States, though this number may be underestimated. PE ranks third behind myocardial infarction and stroke as the leading cause of cardiovascular mortality. Moreover, VTE together costs the United States healthcare system significantly, with an estimated $7-10 billion each year for the treatment and management of this condition. Due to its high incidence, mortality, morbidity, and cost, research has focused on optimizing the management of this serious condition. Endovascular therapy is an emerging field of study in acute PE treatment. These modalities seek to provide minimally invasive techniques while sparing the patient systemic thrombolysis. Currently, the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) gives endovascular therapies an IIa recommendation in patients with hemodynamic deterioration or high-risk patients with contraindications to systemic thrombolysis. Recent studies propose expanded uses for these interventional modalities and purport enhanced effectiveness and improved safety profiles. However, the utilization of these specific treatment strategies varies widely. In fact, amongst the United States Pulmonary Embolism Response Team (PERT) Consortium - an organization that supports the development and formation of multidisciplinary PERT for optimal management of PE - the number using advanced therapies varied from 16-46%. In this review, we review the pathophysiology, risk factors, and diagnostic approach for acute PE. Then, we explore the current PE risk stratification schemata that influence the optimal treatment of acute PE. Next, we examine the various endovascular treatment modalities along with their key research supporting their use. Lastly, we discuss the management of these patients following endovascular treatment and key areas of future research. Risk factors for VTE formation include immobility, trauma, malignancy, infections, and genetic conditions, as they contribute to hypercoagulability, venous stasis, or endothelial injury (Table ). Most PE arise from the proximal veins in the lower extremities as DVTs. These DVTs may fragment and embolize in the venous circulation, which halts within the pulmonary arterial system, resulting in obstruction within the pulmonary circulation. Cardiac failure and hemodynamic compromise often occur in the setting of a large or multiple PE. Pulmonary vascular resistance in the setting of acute PE increases the afterload and stress on the right ventricle (RV), which with time compromises global RV function and ultimately decreases cardiac output. Diagnosis of PE is dependent on a combination of clinical exam, laboratory measures, and imaging. Clinical signs and symptoms of acute PE include dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, cough, pre-syncope or syncope, or hemoptysis. Tachycardia and tachypnea are often present. Hemodynamic instability may be present in the setting of a large or multiple PE. D-dimer is derived from the degradation of cross-linked fibrin and is often elevated in the setting of acute VTE. While D-dimer is very sensitive for PE and has a high negative predictive value, it may be elevated in other conditions as well, including cancer, hospitalized and or critically ill patients, aortic dissection, and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Additionally, laboratory biomarkers such as troponin I or T, brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), or N-terminal (NT)-proBNP may be elevated in acute PE, and are valuable in prognostication and prognosis. Echocardiography is helpful in the risk stratification of an acute PE, as findings of RV overload, dilation, depressed contractility of the RV free wall compared to the apex (McConnell sign) are suggestive of a large PE. Compression ultrasonography (CUS) can be helpful in the diagnosis of PE. In the setting of high clinical suspicion, a positive CUS alone has high specificity for the diagnosis of PE. Electrocardiography may also be helpful in differential diagnosis and prognostication. Various prediction models are available to assess the probability of an acute PE. Models such as the Geneva Score (Table ) and the Wells' Criteria (Table ) stratify patients within low, moderate, and high probabilities of PE based on clinical findings. In patients with a low probability of PE, the Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria (PERC Rule; Table ) may be used in the emergency department (ED) to safely exclude individuals with a low risk of PE, avoid unnecessary testing and treatment. In patients in whom PE cannot be reliably ruled out, computed tomographic pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the preferred method for evaluation of suspected PE. When paired with a low clinical probability, the negative predictive value of CTPA was high at 96%. Despite its accuracy, however, CTPA carries the risk of radiation exposure and contrast nephropathy. When contraindications to CTPA exist, alternative methods include lung scintigraphy (e.g. planar ventilation/perfusion [V/Q] scan). While CTPA was non-inferior to V/Q scan in a randomized control study, V/Q scans are interpreter-dependent and less accurate in determining the exact location of an acute PE, which is crucial when considering an endovascular approach. The Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index and its simplified form (PESI, sPESI, Table 1) are validated risk calculators of mortality and morbidity in patients presenting with acute pulmonary embolism. These scores employ various clinical criteria into a scoring scheme, which predicts 30-day mortality risk. The PESI score divides patients into five classes of 30-day mortality risk, ranging from very low (0-1.6%) to very high mortality (10.0-24.5%). The sPESI divides patients into two categories, the low risk (1.1%) and high risk (8.9%) of 30-day mortality. Studies note that these indices are most reliable in the identification of individuals at low risk for 30-day mortality. The American Heart Association (AHA) previously classified PE severity into three categories. A massive PE is defined as a suspected PE causing hemodynamic collapse manifest as hypotension defined as a sustained systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg for at least 15 minutes or need for inotropic support. Submassive PE is defined as RV strain identified on echocardiography or CTPA (RV/LV ratio >0.9) or RV injury is defined as elevations of cardiac biomarkers without hypotension. Low-risk PE included the individuals not fulfilling the previous criteria. More recently, the ESC divided individuals into 4 groups of 30-day mortality risk (outlined in Table 3). Hemodynamic instability caused by PE is defined as cardiac arrest, obstructive shock systolic BP < 90 mmHg, use of vasopressor support to maintain systolic BP >= 90 mmHg, or a systolic BP drop >=40 mmHg for >15 minutes. RV dysfunction is defined as the presence of echocardiographic findings suggestive of RV strain or failure (e.g. McConnell sign). Unlike the AHA classification, the ESC classification also relies on clinical prognostication through PESI and sPESI calculations. The authors note that the presence of hemodynamic instability combined with RV dysfunction and a confirmed PE is sufficient to classify a patient as high-risk. Differing from the AHA, the ESC does not include BNP and NT-proBNP elevations from the classification scheme, noting that these markers have not been used in prior randomized control trials for treatment decisions. It is important to recognize the classification of acute PE, as they assist in categorizing the treatments appropriate in their management. For simplicity and clarity in treatment indications, this review will categorize individuals based on the ESC guidelines. Barring any contraindications, all individuals with an acute PE should be immediately anticoagulated. Initial choice anticoagulant generally includes unfractionated heparin (UFH), low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), or fondaparinux. Data suggest that LMWH has a lower bleeding risk compared to UFH, though its use may be limited in patients with a creatinine clearance of <=30 mL/min or severe obesity. A randomized control trial of 2213 patients found subcutaneous fondaparinux to be as effective and safe compared to UFH. However, UFH may be preferred in settings of hemodynamic instability, planned surgical intervention, or systemic thrombolysis with tissue-type plasminogen activator (tPA), given its relatively short half-life and availability of a reversal agent. Other considerations such as pregnancy, history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and presence of malignancy should be taken into account before initiation of anticoagulation. Patients with low-risk PE may be transitioned to oral anticoagulants and discharged early for continued treatment at home. Individuals with a high probability for PE, hemodynamic instability, and features of high-risk PE should be considered for reperfusion treatment. Prior management of these PE primarily relied on systemic thrombolytic therapy. This treatment employed tPA, which aimed to rapidly resolve life-threatening pulmonary artery obstructions. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved three types of tPA, including alteplase (i.e. recombinant tPA, rtPA), streptokinase, and urokinase. Both the AHA and ESC favor alteplase 100 mg given over 2 hours compared to streptokinase (250,000 IU loading dose over 30 min, followed by 100,000 IU/h over 12-24 hours) and urokinase (4,400 IU/kg loading dose over 10 min, followed by 4,400 IU/kg/h over 12-24 hours), which are often administered as prolonged infusions. Reduced-dose rtPA has also been investigated and has demonstrated similar efficacy and a possible trend towards an improved safety profile. Various studies demonstrated these improvements compared to UFH alone in the setting of high-risk PE. Systemic thrombolytic therapy can also be used in the intermediate-risk population. The largest randomized controlled trial evaluating this is the Pulmonary Embolism International Thrombolysis (PEITHO) trial. This trial involved 1006 patients randomized into tenecteplase plus heparin versus placebo with heparin. The results demonstrated a significant decrease in all-cause mortality or hemodynamic collapse at 7 days in the tenecteplase group (2.6% vs. 5.6%, P = 0.02). However, there was a larger incidence and significant difference of major bleeding in the tenecteplase group compared to the placebo group. The aforementioned studies and meta-analyses demonstrated that systemic thrombolysis has a mortality benefit in patients with intermediate or high-risk PE. However, systemic thrombolysis is not without its risks. Similar to the findings in the PEITHO trial, various other studies noted the increased frequency of major bleeding in patients treated with systemic thrombolytics compared to UFH alone. This association is also noted within various similar meta-analyses. Because of this, its widespread use may be restrained and restricted to decompensated patients with high-risk PE. Novel interventional therapies for PE seek to provide the thrombolysis benefits at a reduced risk. Various invasive therapies using catheter-based interventions have been used with increasing frequency in recent years. Strategies including catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT), ultrasound-assisted thrombolysis (USAT), mechanical thrombectomy, and rheolytic therapy are used to remove and treat acute PE. The remainder of this review will focus on the current data available for these various treatment modalities. Standard CDT involves the administration of pharmacological thrombolysis with a thrombolytic drug (e.g. tPA) using a standard catheter to directly inject the drug into the pulmonary artery (PA). This may be used in concert with other catheter-directed modalities, such as mechanical fragmentation, aspiration, or maceration. Both Uni-fuse (AngioDynamics Inc, Latham, NY) and Cragg-McNamara (Medtronic, Minneapolis, MN) are two 4F-5F catheters. A similar product named Bashir Endovascular Catheter (Thrombolex, New Britain, PA) is a 7F pharmacomechanical catheter that uses a nitinol-supported infusion basket that can be expanded within the thrombus, allowing for administration of thrombolytic medication at various cross-sectional locations. The FDA approved all three devices for treatment of VTE within the peripheral vasculature, though without a specific indication for PE. A recent feasibility trial demonstrated significant reductions in RV/LV ratio and modified Miller index in patients with acute, intermediate-risk PE when treated with the Bashir Endovascular Catheter. The ongoing prospective trial named tPA by Endovascular Administration for the Treatment of Submassive PE Using CDT for the Reduction of Thrombus Burden (RESCUE) further seeks to define this catheter's use in acute PE (NCT04248868). The RESCUE trial aims to complete in late 2022 and hopes to pave the way for FDA approval of the device in the treatment of acute PE. Randomized controlled trials are currently unavailable for comparison of standard CDT to systemic thrombolysis. Several prospective and retrospective studies have evaluated the efficacy of standard CDT in the treatment of massive and submassive PE. Kuo et al. retrospectively evaluated 12 patients who underwent CDT for massive PE. Seven of these had failed systemic tPA treatment, and the other five had absolute contraindications for systemic tPA. Of the seven, five received alteplase (mean dose 20 mg, range 10-30 mg), and two received tenecteplase (mean dose 12 mg, range 5-20 mg). The procedure was successful in all 12 patients, and the study noted significant improvement in average systolic PA pressures and the Miller index. No major complications such as major bleeding or intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) occurred. The practical application of this study is limited, however, due to the small sample size and concurrent use of rheolytic devices in three of the 12 patients. Patel et al. retrospectively compared 1,169 patients treated with systemic thrombolysis to 352 patients receiving CDT for acute PE. After propensity score matching, CDT was associated with decreased in-hospital mortality and ICH compared to systemic thrombolysis. The generalizability of these conclusions, however, is limited by the study design, lack of differentiation of the different acuities of PE, and absence of information on specific CDT modalities employed. The Pulmonary Embolism Response to Fragmentation, Embolectomy, and Catheter Thrombolysis (PERFECT) trial was a prospective study that evaluated the use of both standard CDT and USAT in the treatment of massive and submassive PE. twenty-eight patients with massive PE and 73 patients with submassive PE were treated with mechanical debulking followed by low-dose hourly tPA infusion via the catheters. 24 of the 28 patients with massive PE were successfully treated (85.7%; 95% CI, 67.3%-96.0%) and 71 of the 73 patients with submassive PE (97.3%; 95% CI, 90.5%-99.7%). Fifty-seven of the 64 with follow up echocardiograms had significant improvement in RV strain (89.1%; 95% CI, 76.8-94.4%), and 78 of 92 with invasive PA pressure monitoring had significant improvement in PA pressures (78 of 92; 95% CI, 75.8-91.4%). There were no reported major bleeding events or ICH within this study population. The PERFECT trial did not demonstrate any significant difference between standard CDT and USAT. USAT is an alternative to the simple infusion catheters of CDT. Currently, the only FDA-approved device is the EKOSonic endovascular system, more commonly known as EKOS (Boston Scientific, Marlborough, MA; Fig. 1). This system uses a specialized 5F catheter with two lumens to concurrently administer thrombolytic medication and ultrasonic waves. In theory, these ultrasonic waves can reversibly disrupt uncrosslinked fibrin fibers, allowing for greater penetration of the thrombolytic medication. This system can be inserted into one or both of the PAs. This system has previously been used to administer thrombolysis between 12-24 hours. Several randomized trials are examining the efficacy of this intervention. The Ultrasound Accelerated Thrombolysis of Pulmonary Embolism (ULTIMA) trial was the first randomized control trial evaluating USAT plus anticoagulation versus anticoagulation alone. The primary endpoint that the researchers evaluated was the difference in the RV/LV ratio from baseline to 24 hours. The USAT group had significant improvement in the RV/LV ratio at 24 hours and was superior to UFH alone in reversing this RV dilation. The SEATTLE II trial (A Prospective, Single-Arm, Multicenter Trial of Ultrasound-Facilitated Catheter-Directed, Low-Dose Fibrinolysis for Acute Massive and Submassive Pulmonary Embolism) was as a prospective trial that involved 150 patients with either acute massive (n = 31) or acute submassive (n = 119) PE. The primary outcome was a change in RV/LV ratio at 48 +/- 6 hours, as well as a primary safety outcome of major bleeding within 72 hours. tPA was administered at a rate of 1 mg/hr for 12-24 hours, for a maximum dose of 24 mg. The trial found that USAT decreased RV/LV ratio by 25% after 48 +/- 6 hours. Moreover, it also noted 17 events of major bleeding within 30 days in 15 patients, with 16 events taking place within 72 hours. There were no reported episodes of ICH. Mandating ultrasound use for establishing venous access and shortening tPA infusions may further decrease the rate of bleeding complications. A randomized, comparative study titled Optimum Duration of Acoustic Pulse Thrombolysis Procedure in Acute Pulmonary Embolism (OPTALYSE PE) evaluated varying doses and durations of tPA infusion during EKOS procedures. This study did not show inferiority with shorter infusion durations of 2, 4, and 6 hours, as well as smaller tPA doses ranging from 4 to 12 mg per lung. The trial suggested that the treatment of acute PE with EKOS could be satisfactorily accomplished in less time and smaller doses of thrombolytics. USAT has also been evaluated for the treatment of PE in numerous retrospective and nonrandomized studies. A recent meta-analysis by Pei et al. evaluated these in conjunction with the above randomized control studies. This meta-analysis appraised 28 studies, which included 1,430 patients treated with USAT. Most studies used a maximum total dose of 24 mg of tPA for 12-24 hours. These authors noted significant improvements in RV/LV ratio and mean pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP) in patients presenting with either massive or submassive PE treated with USAT. USAT was noted to be relatively safe as well, with a total in-hospital mortality rate of 2.9%, a major bleeding rate of 5.4%, and a minor bleeding rate of 6.0%. This is a lower rate compared to the rate found in the PEITHO study, which noted an 11.5% rate of major bleeding and 32.6% rate of minor bleeding in the systemic tenecteplase group when compared to placebo. Future research has focused on comparing standard CDT to USAT. The drawback to USAT is the cost of the equipment, whereas standard CDT catheters are often cheaper in comparison. Two retrospectives analyses have compared USAT to standard CDT. Rothschild et al. evaluated 98 (62 USAT vs. 36 CDT) cases of massive and intermediate-risk PE. After 24 hours, PASP decreased and RV/LV ratio improved in both groups without a statistically significant difference. ICU and hospital length of stay (LOS) were similar in the two groups, and there was a nonsignificant trend towards lesser bleeding in the CDT group compared to the USAT group. Similarly, Rao et al. evaluated 37 patients undergoing USAT compared to 33 undergoing standard CDT admitted for submassive and massive PE. There was a similar and nonsignificant decrease in RV systolic pressure, comparable hospital LOS, bleeding complications, and quality of life (QOL) as assessed by the Short-Form Health Survey (SF-36). Taken together, these retrospective studies fail to demonstrate a significant benefit of USAT over CDT. A recent randomized control trial called Standard vs. UltrasouNd-assiSted CathEter Thrombolysis for Submassive Pulmonary Embolism (SUNSET sPE) aimed to comparing the CDT and USAT in patients presenting with acute submassive PE. Preliminary results suggest there was no significant difference between the two groups in mean thrombus score reduction, obstruction index. However, there was a significant difference in the change of RV/LV ratio from baseline at 48 hours favoring the USAT group. Additionally, the average infusion times in both arms were 14 hours, with two reports of major bleeds (1 ICH, 1 vaginal bleed). Although final results are not yet available, it would be interesting to assess if shorter infusion durations as used in the OPTALYSE trial could achieve similar efficacy with decreased bleeding risk. In conclusion, numerous studies have demonstrated the favorable efficacy and safety profile of USAT in the treatment of high or intermediate-risk PE. However, the limited data available has not been able to demonstrate a significant difference in outcomes when compared to standard CDT. Mechanical thrombectomy involves the use of specialized catheters to aspirate or vacuum suction PE. The theoretical benefit of such interventions over other catheter-based interventions is the removal of PE without the use of thrombolytic medications, thus reducing the bleeding risk. There are many different catheters commercially available. This review will focus on some of the more commonly used systems. The Pronto Extraction Catheters (Vascular Solutions, Inc. Minneapolis, MN) is FDA approved for the treatment of embolism, without a specific indication for treatment of acute PE. Limited data are available for the use of Pronto catheters for the treatment of this condition. Heberlein et al. reported successful removal of PE and improvement in mean pulmonary pressures in 8 of 10 patients treated with the 0.035" and XL extraction catheters. No deaths were reported immediately following the procedure, though 30- day mortality was high (6 of 9, 67%). The XL catheter is no longer commercially available, though newer versions such as the LP, V3, and V4 catheters are currently used. Currently, no study has evaluated their uses in acute PE. The Aspirex MAX 7-11F catheters (Straub Medical, Wangs, Switzerland) are FDA-approved devices for the extraction of embolic material without a specific indication for acute PE. This device employs a high-speed rotating spiral at the catheter tip that creates a negative pressure system that macerates and aspirates the thrombus. A retrospective study of 36 patients with massive and submassive PE treated with Aspirex demonstrated complete removal of PE in 30 (83.3%) of patients, in addition to a significant decrease in mean PAP. Survival immediately following the procedure was high at 94.4% (34) and 360-day follow-up (88.8%, 32). The AngioVac system (AngioDynamics, Latham, NY) consists of a 23F catheter with a proprietary funnel tip connected to a veno-veno bypass circuit. The catheter creates suction to remove the intravascular clot, which traps the material in a filter within the inflow tract. The filtered blood is returned to the body via the outflow tract 18F catheter. This system is often used to remove thrombus or embolic material from the iliofemoral veins, inferior and superior vena cava, and right atrium. The AngioVac system has been used for the treatment of acute PE as well; however, data for its use is limited to small, single-center case and retrospective studies. Moreover, these studies have noted the technical difficulty with the device during PE removal, as the catheter size creates difficultly maneuvering to the PA. Hence, removal of a distal clot is often unsuccessful using this system. Additionally, one study noted a right ventricular free wall perforation, resulting in death. A smaller aspiration catheter called the Indigo Thrombectomy System (Penumbra, Inc. Alameda CA; Fig. 2) uses a continuous vacuum pump to extract thrombus. Unlike the AngioVac system, Indigo does not use a veno-veno bypass to return aspirated blood to the body. Rather, a proprietary thrombus removal algorithm differentiates between patent and occluded blood flow. Patent blood flow triggers the system to intermittently aspirate. When the clot is engaged, the system automatically transitions to continuous aspiration. Previously, data on its effectiveness were limited to single- center, retrospective studies. However, a recent multi-center, prospective study titled Evaluating the Safety and Efficacy of the Indigo aspiration system in Acute Pulmonary Embolism (EXTRACT-PE) found the system to be safe and effective in the management of acute PE. One hundred nineteen patients enrolled in this study presented with either submassive (118) or massive (1) PE. There was a significant decrease in the mean reduction of RV/LV ratio and mean PASP at 48 hours. Furthermore, adverse events were rare, with only 2 patients experiencing 3 events (hemoptysis, access site bleeding, ventricular arrhythmia). Of them, only 1 patient died following the procedure (0.8%). This study concluded that the system was safe and effective for the management of acute PE. More recently, Penumbra has released its newest catheter named Lightning 12, which boasts of a large 0.131" lumen, angled tip, and improved design of increased trackability and torqueability. The FlowTriever System (Inari Medical, Irvine, CA, Fig. 3) includes a 16, 20, or 24F aspiration catheter and the FlowTriever catheter. The aspiration catheter is first used to vacuum suction PE within the PA. If the clot remains, the specialized FlowTriever catheter (available in 4 sizes ranging from 6-25 mm) is inserted through the aspiration catheter and engages the clot. This catheter has three self-expanding nitinol mesh disks that are designed to trap the clot and draw it back through the aspiration catheter. The eminent FlowTriever Pulmonary Embolectomy Clinical Study (FLARE) was the initial prospective, multi-center, single-arm trial that provided FDA clearance of this device for use in acute PE. One hundred six patients presenting with acute intermediate-risk PE were treated with the system. This study assessed the primary endpoints of change in RV/LV ratio at 48 hours, as well the primary safety endpoint of major adverse events (MAEs), a composite score of events such as death, major bleeding, device-related pulmonary or cardiac injury, and clinical deterioration within 48 hours. At 48 hours, 101 patients (95.3%) had a significant decrease in RV/LV ratio. The procedure was well tolerated, with only 4 patients (3.8%) experiencing 6 MAEs (1 major bleeding, 1 pulmonary vascular injury, 4 clinical deterioration). Additionally, the authors noted a significant decrease in mean PAP. These authors concluded that FlowTriever is both safe and effective for the management of acute, intermediate-risk PE. Several retrospective studies since the FLARE study have reported similar outcomes. These studies indicated a significant reduction in mean PAP, as well as low mortality and technical success. Moreover, these retrospective studies also included patients presenting with high-risk PE, suggesting a possible expanded use of the system. Ongoing studies aim to add further data for the use of FlowTriever in the management of acute PE. The FlowTriever All-Comer Registry for Patient Safety and Hemodynamics (FLASH) study (NCT03761173) is an ongoing observational study evaluating the rate of MAE (device-related death, major bleeding, device or procedure-related adverse events) in up to 500 patients presenting with acute PE. Initial 30-day data suggest a significant reduction in mean PAP, low rate of major bleeding (n=2, 1%, both not ICH), and low 30-day mortality (n=1, 0.6%, unrelated to procedure). The study aims to complete at the end of 2021. Additionally, the FlowTriever for Acute Massive Pulmonary Embolism (FLAME) is a study in development. This study seeks to define the role of FlowTriever in the treatment of high-risk PE compared to standard care. A completion date for this study is not yet available. Rheolytic thrombectomy (RT) involves the use of a single catheter with a high-speed, pressurized saline jet stream emitted through the distal catheter tip. This creates a vacuum, which macerates the thrombus and draws the clot particles out from the vessel into the catheter. The most commonly used device is the AngioJet Rheolytic Thrombectomy System (Boston Scientific, Marlborough, MA). AngioJet has been used for the removal of clot burden from arterio-venous fistulas, grafts, and distal vessels. The AngioJet system has also been evaluated for the treatment of acute PE. However, data for this use are limited to mostly small case series and retrospective studies. AngioJet has been associated with several adverse outcomes, including bradyarrhythmias, major bleeding, and intraprocedural hemoptysis. Because of this, the FDA has issued a black-box warning recommending against the use of AngioJet in the treatment of acute pulmonary embolism. Patients following interventional therapies for PE should be anticoagulated before discharge. Guidelines recommend >=3 months of anticoagulation for all patients with PE, though a longer duration may be necessary provided various risk factors are present. Currently, there are no studies that have examined the optimal anticoagulant following interventional PE therapies. However, several studies have compared direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs) to vitamin K antagonists (VKAs) and found that DOACs are non-inferior to VKAs in the treatment of PE. However, LMWH is often initiated for the treatment of PE in the setting of pregnancy or cancer. While research suggests that systemic thrombolysis is associated with a 60% reduction in recurrent PE compared to anticoagulation alone (OR, 0.4 [95% CI, 0.22-0.]), it remains unclear if endovascular therapies for PE have a similar benefit. Further research is required to determine if catheter-directed therapies reduce the rate of subsequent PE. Many patients may develop persistent symptoms and decreased quality of life despite adequate treatment of PE. Due to the limited data available, it remains unclear as to whether catheter-based interventions significantly improve QOL after treatment of PE. Piazza et al. examined the 1-year changes in RV remodeling, functional status, and quality of life in the patients treated in the OPTALYSE-PE trial. All four study arms of this trial had improvements in the RV/LV diameter ratio at 1-year follow-up. This mirrored similar improvements in the 6-minute walk test and QOL questionnaires. As previously mentioned, Rao et al. did not find any significant difference in QOL between USAT and CDT at 3 years. However, this cohort was not directly compared to systemic anticoagulation or thrombolysis. Further data are required to determine the effect of catheter-based interventions on symptomology and QOL following hospitalization. Remnants of the unresolved thromboembolic disease may lead to late pulmonary complications such as chronic thromboembolic disease (CTED) and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH). These serious, longstanding complications may lead to a significant reduction in quality of life and survival rates and are areas of emerging research and treatment. However, there is currently a lack of evidence suggesting a significant reduction in rates of CTEPH catheter-directed treatments. Further prospective studies are needed to evaluate the effects of catheter-based interventions on these outcomes.

content: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is currently the 4th leading cause of death worldwide and 2nd in India. Patients with COPD may present with acute worsening of their respiratory symptoms known as acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD). In addition to increased morbidity and health-care utilization, AE-COPD significantly reduces both in-hospital and long-term survival. Majority (50%-70%) of the events of AECOPD are precipitated by respiratory tract infections, followed by exposure to environmental pollution (10%). However, in up to 30% of cases, the cause of exacerbation remains unknown. Various studies have reported COPD as one of the independent risk factors for venous thromboembolism (VTE). In a systematic review and meta-analysis, the pooled prevalence of pulmonary embolism (PE) in unexplained AECOPD was reported to be 16.1%. In a recent multicenter cross-sectional study (n = 740), the prevalence of PE was 5.9% (11% in patients with suspicion of PE and 4.3% in patients with no suspicion of PE on initial assessment). However, higher prevalence of PE was reported in postmortem studies ranging from 28% to 51%. In addition, patients of COPD with PE have significantly higher 3 month as well as 1 year mortality compared to patients with PE alone. It is therefore important to identify PE as a cause of AECOPD, as delay in diagnosis and treatment is associated with poorer outcome. As the symptoms of AECOPD are nonspecific, it is often difficult to differentiate PE as a cause of AECOPD based on clinical examination alone. Multidetector computed tomography (MDCT) pulmonary angiography (PA) is currently the investigation of choice in suspected PE. The reported prevalence of spirometrically defined COPD (in adults >= 40 years) in our part of world is 17.3% in males and 14.8% in females. It is higher than that reported from other states of our country and various parts of the world. We have previously reported that viral respiratory tract infections are responsible for acute exacerbation in sizable number of our COPD patients. However, the cause of AECOPD remains unknown in a large number of patients. With this background, the present study was designed to know the prevalence of PE in patients with AECOPD with no identifiable etiology requiring hospitalization at a tertiary care hospital of Kashmir in North India. This study was a prospective observational study that was conducted over a period of 2 years in Sheri-Kashmir institute of medical sciences, a multidisplinary institute of north India, an 800-bedded hospital. Patients of COPD who presented with AE-COPD to the emergency department of our institute severe enough to require hospitalization were assessed for the eligibility criteria. Patients of AECOPD with no obvious cause on initial assessment were included in the study. Following assessments were done to rule out the possible etiology of worsening of symptoms in patients with COPD: (a) history of fever, purulent sputum, myalgias, and running nose to rule out possibility of infective etiology; (b) chest radiography was done to look for the evidence of pneumothorax, pleural effusion, or pulmonary edema as a cause of exacerbation of symptoms. (c) Electrocardiography to look for any evidence suggestive of acute coronary syndrome and arrhythmias. Those with definite alternative cause of worsening of symptoms (like respiratory tract infection, pneumothorax, and myocardial ischemia) plus requiring mechanical ventilation or who fail to give consent were excluded from the study. Diagnosis of COPD was made based on the compatible history and postbronchodilator forced expiratory volume in 1 s to forced vital capacity ratio of <0.7. Severity of COPD as well as exacerbation of COPD was defined as per the global initiative for chronic obstructive lung disease (GOLD) criteria. In addition to routine investigations that included complete blood count, biochemistry, chest radiograph, and arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis, a detailed history, physical examination, the use of pretest probability scoring (simplified Geneva scoring [SGS]), and qualitative D-dimer assay were carried out in all the participants. Compression ultrasound (CUS) and venous Doppler of lower extremities were performed for the presence of deep venous thrombosis (DVT) followed by MDCT PA for PE. Reporting of CUS/Doppler study of lower extremities and MDCT-PA was done by a radiologist with more than 10-year experience in a teaching tertiary care center [Figure 1]. Noncompressibility or incomplete compressibility of deep veins of lower extremities on CUS was taken as criteria for the presence of DVT. Computed tomography pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) was considered positive for PE if there was a total occlusion of the vessel by a low attenuation material or presence of an intraluminal defect surrounded by a contrast material. Patients were considered to have PE if they had positive CTPA or positive CUS/Doppler of lower extremities plus high clinical suspicion (if CTPA was not done due to any contraindication). PE was excluded in case of negative CTPA and/or lower extremity CUS/Doppler. History regarding the presence of risk factors for VTE including the presence of malignancy, immobility, recent surgery, or previous VTE was recorded. Patients who had DVT or PTE were managed with therapeutic anticoagulation and those with PE who fulfilled the criteria for thrombolysis, received thrombolysis as per the standard protocol. AECOPD was managed as per the available GOLD guidelines. The study protocol was approved by departmental ethics committee. A written consent was obtained from all patients who participated in the study. All continuous variables were expressed as the mean +- standard deviation in case of normally distributed data and were compared using unpaired Student's t-test. The difference between the two groups was assessed using Chi-square or Fisher's exact test. Multiple logistic regression analysis was performed to identify the predictors of PE. A P < 0.05 was considered to indicate significance. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS version 20.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, Illinois, USA). The 100 cases included 57% (n = 57) were males and 43% (n = 43) were females with a mean age of 66.32 +- 14.06 years. Majority of the patients (69%) belonged to age group of more than 60 years with no difference between the two groups. The demographic data of the participants are depicted in Table 1. PE was observed in 14% (n = 14) of participants. CTPA for PE was positive in 13% (n = 13) of cases, while as one patient died before CTPA was done but had DVT on CUS/Doppler. Among the participants with PE, 63% (n = 9) had the concomitant presence of lower extremity DVT. In majority of the patients (46%) with PE, thrombus was seen in main pulmonary artery, followed by segmental (38.5%) and at subsegmental (15%) level [Table 2]. None of the cases with negative CTPA had DVT on CUS/Doppler lower limbs. No significant difference was observed between severity of AECOPD and presence of PE (P = 0.521) [Table 1]. All patients of AECOPD (irrespective of presence or absence of PE) were classified as having high risk for PE based on SGS. However, patients with PE had significantly higher values compared to patients without PE (5.57 +- 1.158 in patients with PE vs. 3.49 +- 0.592 in patients without PE, P < 0.001). No significant difference was observed between two groups in terms of age, sex distribution, and risk factors for embolism except for previous history of VTE (35.7%, 5/14 in patients with PE vs. 12.8%, 11/86 in patients with no PE, P = 0.03) [Table 1]. Significant difference was observed in clinical presentation and vital signs among patients of AECOPD with and without PE. Hemoptysis was present in 35.7% (5 out of 14) of patients with PE and only in 7% (6 out of 84) of patients with no evidence of PE (P = 0.001). Chest pain was the presenting complaint in 92.9% (13 out of 14) of patients with PE compared to 38.4% (33 out of 84) of patients with no PE (P = 0.001). Patients with PE were more likely to have tachycardia (heart rate [HR] >100/min), tachypnea (respiratory rate [RR] >30/min), and hypotension (systolic blood pressure [SBP] <100 mmHg) on presentation as compared to patients with no evidence of PE. No significant difference was observed in terms of laboratory parameters between the two groups, except patients with PE tend to have respiratory alkalosis (pH >7.45: 78.6% vs. 4.3% P <= 0.001 and PCO2 <=45: 71.4% vs. 3.4% P <= 0.001) and low platelet count (<1.5 l/cumm: 85.7% vs. 36.6%, P <= 0.001). Qualitative D-dimer assay was done in all the participants. No difference was observed in terms of percentage of positive Dimer test in both the groups (92.85% in patients with PE vs. 90.6% of patients without PE, P = 0.694) [Table 1]. The presence of previous history of VTE, hemoptysis, chest pain, simplified Geneva score of more than 5, disproportionate tachypnea (RR >30/min), tachycardia (HR >100/min), hypotension (SBP <100 mmHg), and respiratory alkalosis were significantly associated with PE in patients with AECOPD on univariate analysis [Table 3]. However, on multivariate binary logistic regression, the presence of respiratory alkalosis with PCO2 <45 mmHg and pH >7.45 predicted PE in patients with AECOPD. Out of 13 cases of AECOPD with PE, 38.46% (n = 5) fulfilled the criteria for thrombolysis. Majority of these patients (80%, n = 4) had thrombus in main pulmonary artery. Streptokinase infusion was used as an agent for systemic thrombolysis in 4 (80%) patients and t-PA in 1 (20%) patient. Four out of five (80%) patients who received thrombolysis improved clinically with hemodynamic stability. Remaining patients of PE (n = 8) who did not require thrombolysis were managed with anticoagulation alone in addition to standard of care for the management of AECOPD. Total of eight patients died during hospitalization. No significant difference was noted with regard to the in-hospital mortality between the two groups (5.81%, n = 5 in patients without PE vs. 14.28%, n = 2 in patients with PE, P = 0.25). The present study showed the prevalence of PE in patients with AECOPD of unknown etiology to be 14%. The prevalence of PE in COPD patients with unknown etiology varies from as low as 2% to as high as 29.1%. Tillie-Leblond et al. reported that 15 out of 60 (25%) patients with AECOPD of unknown etiology had PE. Similarly, Gunen et al. reported 29.1% prevalence of PE in patients with AECOPD of unknown reason. However, in a study by Rutschmann et al., the prevalence of PE was only 3.3%. The low prevalence of PE might be due to selection bias excluding patients with D-dimer level <500 mug/l and with low clinical probability of PE. A study from India and Korea reported the prevalence of PE to be 2% and 5%, respectively. In a meta-analysis that included seven studies have shown that the pooled prevalence of PE in unexplained AE-COPD was 16.1% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 8.3%-25.8%). These differences could be due to number of reasons that may include difference in sample size, enrollment criteria, study design, or diagnostic modalities used (V/Q scan vs. CTPA). Various validated bedside clinical prediction scores are being used to predict the likelihood of PE and to reduce the need for imaging. We observed that the use of clinical prediction score (simplified Geneva score) was not useful in predicting PE in patients with AECOPD. In our study, all patients with AECOPD had simplified Geneva score of >2, indicating high likelihood of PE, but only 13% of patients (13/100) had evidence of PE. However, a significant difference was noted in patients with and without PE if mean values of SGS were considered (5.57 +- 1.16 in patients with PE vs. 3.49 +- 0.59 in patients without PE, P <= 0.001). Therefore, likelihood of PE was significantly higher in patients of AECOPD with SGS of more than 5. Gunen et al.reported that none of the patients with low clinical prediction score and about 20% of patients with moderate score had PE. However, various studies have shown that patients of COPD with PE had lower pretest probability for PE using various PE predicting scores. These observations showed that the use of clinical prediction scoring system can be misleading when used in patients of COPD in predicting PE. We did not observe a significant association of PE in patients with AECOPD of unknown etiology with well-known risk factors except previous history of VTE. Studies have shown that, among various risk factors for PE, the presence of previous history of venous thrombosis was more likely to be associated with PE (P value 0.04, RR 0.26, 95% CI, 0.07-0.93). Tillie-Leblond et al. reported that in addition to previous history of VTE, presence of malignancy was associated with higher risk of PE (risk ratio, 1.82 [CI, 1.13-2.92]). Laurent Bet al. concluded that COPD patients with a history of venous thromboembolism, especially previous PE has increased risk of recurrence of PE and fatal PE as compared to those presenting with DVT alone. The most common symptom of PE is breathlessness at rest and with exertion, orthopnea, pleuritic chest pain, wheezing, cough, and hemoptysis, whereas the most common signs include tachypnea, tachycardia, decreased breath sounds, or accentuated second heart sound. Although symptoms of AECOPD due to PE are nonspecific, previous studies have reported that chest pain was more frequently reported by patients of AECOPD with PE as compared to patients with no PE. Our study revealed that, among clinical features, the presence of pleuritic chest pain and hemoptysis significantly predicted PE as a cause of AECOPD compared to other symptoms (P=). However, few studies have failed to show any significant difference of symptoms in patients of AECOPD with and without PE. The result of a recent meta-analysis that evaluated the prevalence of PE in patients of unknown etiology showed that, in patients with AE-COPD, the presence of pleuritic chest pain significantly predicted the presence of PE. Patients with peripheral pulmonary embolus usually present with chest pain and hemoptysis. In a series of 172 patients who presented with AECOPD secondary to PE, the most common symptom reported was pleuritic chest pain. About 80% of patients with PE had peripheral pulmonary embolus. However, contrary to this, our study reported that 92.8% (n = 13) of patients with CTPA documented PE, presented with chest pain and 42.8%of these had centrally located thrombus. Similar findings were reported by Gunen et al. in his study. These findings can be explained by the fact that massive centrally located PE can cause ischemic chest pain from right ventricular infarction. There was a significant difference in terms of physical examination findings in patients of AECOPD with and without PE. Tachycardia (HR >100/min), tachypnea (RR > 30/min), and hypotension (SBP of < 100 mmHg) was present in significantly higher percentage of AECOPD patients with PE compared to patients with no PE. Our findings were in consistent with those reported by previous studies. Hence, the suspicion of PE should be kept higher in patients of AECOPD with disproportionate tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypotension. Patients of COPD with acute exacerbation may present with either hypercapnic or hypoxemic respiratory failure. In the acute setting, hypercapnea may be increased secondary to increased dead space ventilation and ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch caused by increased mucus production and bronchial constriction. In patients with PE, ABG usually reveals hypoxemia, hypocapnia, and respiratory alkalosis. We observed that patients of AECOPD with PE had significantly lower levels of paCO2 and higher pH compared to patients with no PE. These findings may be due to reflex tachypnea associated with PE secondary to increase in dead space ventilation. Our findings were in consistent with those reported by Tillie-Leblond et al., they observed that a decrease of paCO2 of at least 5 mmHg from baseline was the only ABG abnormality associated with PE. Rodger et al. and Lippmann and Fein. also suggested that a decrease in paCO2 during COPD exacerbation might indicate PE. On the other hand, no reduction in paCO2 was reported in patients of AECOPD with PE by Lesser et al. and Mispelaere et al. It is to be noted that Shaker et al. observed that patients of AE-COPD with PE had hypercapnia rather than hypocapnia. These observations can be attributed to increased dead space ventilation and respiratory muscle fatigue present during AECOPD. Although majority of the patients with PE have hypoxemia, no significant difference was observed between two groups in this study. Jerald et al. and Hatem et al. reported that patients of COPD with PE tend to have greater decrease in PaO2 than patients with PE alone. However, Stein et al. observed that hypoxemia can be absent or minimal in patients with PE. About 18% of patients with PE can have PaO2 between 85 mmHg and 105 mmHg and up to 6% of patients with PE have normal alveolar arterial gradient for oxygen. PE and DVT represent the spectrum of same disease. About 80% of patients with PE have evidence of DVT of lower extremities. Our study showed that 64.3% (9/13) of patients with PE had DVT of lower extremities on CUS. Absence of DVT in 30.76% of patients with PE could be due to in situ thrombus formation in pulmonary arteries or embolization of entire thrombus from lower extremities or thrombus involving iliac vessels. Kamel et al. reported that only 26.7% of patients with PE had DVT on CUS and suggested an alternative etiology for pulmonary thrombosis such as hypoxemia and polycythemia. Our study has some limitations. First, only qualitative D-dimer assay was performed that could be responsible for excessive use of CTPA and may explain lesser prevalence of PE as compared to previous studies. Secondly patients of AECOPD requiring invasive mechanical ventilation were excluded that could be associated with selection bias and lesser prevalence. Also it was a single-center study that was performed in a place with higher prevalence of COPD and therefore may not represent the true scenario of other places of the country. A small sample size would also call for a larger study on a country wide basis to ascertain the true burden of the disease so as to modulate the management accordingly.

title: Prevalence and predictors of pulmonary embolism in patients with acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

content: Acute pulmonary embolism (PE) is one of the most common diseases of the cardiovascular system. It is estimated that PE occurs at a frequency of 39-115/100,000 population/year and causes over 400,000 deaths in Europe every year. It is the third most frequent vascular disease, after myocardial infarction and stroke. The clinical presentation of PE is heterogenous: from mild impairment of exercise tolerance (low-risk PE), through severe dyspnoe with symptoms of right ventricular overload (intermediate-risk PE) to hemodynamic collapse, "obstructive" shock and death (high-risk patients) most often related to acute insufficiency of the right ventricle (RV) and respiratory failure. Although most patients with PE can be successfully treated with anticoagulants, hemodynamically unstable patients require urgent systemic thrombolysis (ST). Thrombolytic therapy, however, has significant limitations. First of all, it is associated with a significant increase in the risk of major bleeding (13%), including up to 3% of patients treated with ST, who have dangerous intracranial bleeding, mainly cerebral hemorrhagic stroke. In the group of patients of the ZATPOL : Polish national prospective registry, it has been shown that the occurrence of major bleeding in acute PE significantly worsened the prognosis. In high-risk (hemodynamically unstable) patients, the clinical benefit of thrombolysis exceeds the risk of bleeding, but in intermediate-risk patients the potential clinical benefit of ST does not balance the risk of major bleeding and does not reduce mortality. On the other hand, about 5-10% of patients who are initially hemodynamically stable may experience a sudden and unexpected clinical deterioration. According to the guidelines of the European Society of Cardiology, in the case of contraindications to thrombolysis or its failure, surgical embolectomy is recommended. However, a severe preoperative condition and high incidence of comorbidities, as well as limited availability of cardiac surgery result in high mortality in this group. Furthermore, it has been shown that thrombolytic therapy is often not used in high-risk patients, even though there are no contraindications. Moreover, in intermediate-high-risk patients, the decision on thrombolysis or surgical therapy is often taken too late, and hemodynamic deterioration in this group of patients is associated with high mortality. Consequently, new techniques for transcatheter invasive treatment of PE (catheter-directed therapy [CDT]) have been developed, which can remove thrombi from the pulmonary arteries without the additional risks posed by systemic thrombolysis or cardiac surgery. In the last decade, many new devices and techniques have been proposed for transcatheter treatment of PE. There is also a growing number of scientific data from clinical observational studies and registries confirming the clinical effectiveness of interventional treatment with a reduction in the number of patients with significant bleeding. However, only few randomized trials comparing CDT with standard anticoagulant and thrombolytic therapy are available in the literature. Nonetheless, quick and correct diagnosis, proper risk stratification and selection of optimal therapy from a constantly growing pharmacological and intervention armamentarium, seems to be crucial in patients with acute PE. In 2013, in Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston (United States), the world's first multispecialist team was created for quick consultation and selection of the therapy in patients with PE. This team was named the Pulmonary Embolism Response Team (PERT). The PERT concept was based on a combination of two other proven clinical practice models: The Heart Team and the Rapid Response Team. The growing role of PERTs in making individual therapeutic decisions is pointed out, especially in hemodynamically unstable patients with contraindications to thrombolysis (e.g. with active bleeding shortly after surgery) or with significant co-morbidities (including cancers), as well as in patients with intermediate-high risk patients in whom this treatment may accelerate clinical improvement and improve prognosis. Treatment methods should also include various methods of CDT as an alternative to ST and surgical embolectomy. The current guidelines of the European Society of Cardiology recommended set-up (class recommendations IIa/level of evidence C) of in-hospital PERTs adapted to local resources and access to specialists. The purpose of this document is to define the standards of PERT under Polish conditions, based on the experience of teams already operating in Poland, which was formed in April 2019 an agreement called the Polish PERT Initiative (PPI). The goals of PPI are improving the treatment of patients with PE at local, regional and national levels, involving gathering, assessing and sharing of data on the effectiveness of PE treatment (including various types of CDT), disseminating the knowledge about optimal treatment of PE, optimizing financing of procedures in this area, creating expert documents and supporting scientific research, as well as cooperating with other communities and scientific societies. A clear organization model of PERT has yet to be defined. The world's first PERT from Massachusetts General Hospital involved specialists from various fields, serving for immediate consultation and selection of therapy in patients with PE. The first PERT served as a model for other medical centers and soon these centers combined their experience within the National PERT Consortium. The data presented by the PERT Consortium shows a vast diversity in the organization of teams and the patient population they are dealing with. The essence of PERT's activity is to coordinate the diagnostic and therapeutic process of patients with PE of severe or atypical course by choosing the optimal management strategy based on the expert knowledge of a multidisciplinary team of specialists of whom it is comprised. The PERT coordinator should be continuously available by phone (24/7) on a dedicated phone number and after accepting the application must be able to organize quick consultations (< 30 min) with relevant specialists. These consultations may be a teleconference, during which all participants have access to a patient's medical data and imaging tests. The PERT should include specialists with practical experience in the treatment of acute PE using various methods, as well as experts to assist in case of complications or the presence of comorbidities that require modification of standard methods of acute PE. Among the physicians directly involved in the process of treating a patient upon PERT care there are usually specialists who have experience in the field of intensive cardiac therapy, echocardiography and interventional cardiology, as well as cardiac surgeons, specialists in emergency medicine, anesthesiologists and radiologists, including interventional radiologists. The second group of specialists whose consultations may be necessary in selected cases should include neurologists, neurosurgeons, oncologists, vascular surgeons, hematologists and specialists in lung disease. It seems that the specialists listed in the first group should constitute a permanent PERT team. However, the final composition of PERT varies between centers and depends on resources and experience. The most important tasks of PERT in the acute phase of PE include choosing optimal pharmacotherapy (including determining indications or contraindications for thrombolysis), interventional treatment (thrombus fragmentation, CDT, venous filter implantation) or cardiac surgery (pulmonary embolectomy). For those reasons, the ideal organizational solution is to create PERT in hospitals with all available treatment options in one location. If PERT is located in a hospital without a cardiac surgery department, it should have the formal cooperation with a cardiac surgery center ensuring the possibility of immediate transfer of patients for further treatment. Optimally, every PERT should have access to treatment with extra corporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) device, which is the equipment of cardiac surgery departments in Poland. In addition to the acute phase of PE treatment, the role of PERT may be to support the optimization of management in subsequent months, including determining the method and duration of chronic anticoagulation, possible implantation of the inferior vena cava filter and patient monitoring for the occurrence of chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH). Hemodynamically unstable patients, i.e. with systemic hypotension, in shock, requiring infusion of catecholamines or cardiopulmonary resuscitation constitute a group of patients with high risk of early death with early mortality exceeding 15% and contain about 5% of patients with PE. Hypotonia is defined as systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg or a decrease in systolic blood pressure of at least 40 mmHg for > 15 min if it is not associated with new arrhythmias, hypovolemia or sepsis. Confirmation of the diagnosis of high-risk PE is not only the finding of RV dysfunction in echocardiographic or tomographic assessment. Patients with high-risk PE require immediate reperfusion treatment. Systemic thrombolysis in high-risk PE patients is recommended as class I (evidence level B), surgical embolectomy as class I recommendation (evidence level C), and catheter-directed therapy as class IIa recommendation (evidence level C). Among initially hemodynamically stable patients with the presence of RV overload and positive markers of myocardial overload, 5-10% will develop hemodynamic instability despite anticoagulation. Therefore, patients with intermediate-high-risk PE at an early stage of hospitalization require monitoring, preferably in an intensive care unit. In the case of hemodynamic instability, it is advisable to implement thrombolytic treatment (class I recommendation/evidence level B), for which the alternative is surgical embolectomy or CDT (class IIa recommendation/evidence level C). The Bova scale allows the identification of patients at risk of decompensation and death dependent on PE from among initially stable hemodynamically stable patients. At the beginning of transcatheter therapy for a patient with PE, a pulmonary artery angiography from the femoral or internal jugular vein should be performed initially using 5-7 F diameter pigtail catheters. Pulmonary angiography enables visualization of thrombi not only in the main pulmonary, lobar or segmental arteries but even in smaller (subsegmental) vessels. During pulmonary angiography, hemodynamic measurements should be made in the right atrium and right ventricle, and the pulmonary trunk to assess the severity of PE and exclude the overlapping of acute PE on CTEPH. Mechanical reperfusion involves the introduction of a catheter into the pulmonary arteries from the femoral or internal jugular vein to remove thrombi and reduce pulmonary resistance, facilitate the return of RV function, improve the patient's clinical condition and prognosis. Percutaneous embolectomy involves a variety of methods, from mechanical thrombus fragmentation, to thrombus aspiration and a pharmacomechanical approach of mechanical or ultrasound-assisted thrombus fragmentation with local administration of reduceddose thrombolysis. Before the procedure, one should perform echocardiographic examination not only to assess RV function, but also to exclude thrombi in the right heart cavities and exclude thrombosis in the punctured femoral vein. In the published meta-analysis of Bajaj et al., periprocedural success, defined as hemodynamic stabilization, reduction of hypoxia and discharge from hospital, was achieved in 87% of patients treated with endovascular treatment. The first Polish experiences with transcatheter methods (AngioJet system, Indigo Penumbra aspiration thrombectomy, EKOS system and Cleaner system) have recently been published. Another interventional technique supporting the treatment of acute PE is the implantation of vascular filters into the inferior vena cava. Venous filters protect the patient's pulmonary arteries from subsequent embolism from deep veins of the lower extremities or the pelvic venous plexus. The results of PREPIC studies indicate that venous filters reduce the incidence of PE, while slightly increasing the incidence of venous thrombosis, without reducing overall mortality. In a recent analysis of the database of an American health fund, which included 16,950 patients with PE and concomitant cancer, a venous filter was used in 19% of patients. A reduction of mortality was demonstrated in a group of patients > 60 years of age in whom the filter was implanted, in relation to the group of conservatively treated patients. Current European Society of Cardiology guidelines recommend the implantation of venous filters in patients with PE and absolute contraindications to anticoagulation or in patients who have recurrent PE despite adequate treatment (class IIa recommendation/evidence level C). Currently, the standard is an application of retrievable filters, which can be used in patients with PE or venous thrombosis before extensive surgery requiring temporary cessation of anticoagulation. After stabilization of the patient's condition and resolution of contraindications to anticoagulation, removal of the filter should always be considered. Depending on the type of filter, it can be removed up to 6 months after implantation. In high-risk PE, surgical pulmonary embolectomy should be used in patients with absolute contraindications to thrombolytic therapy or if it is ineffective and should be considered in selected patients at intermediate risk. A separate group consists of patients with thrombi passing from the right atrium to the left side through the patent foramen ovale. Pulmonary embolectomy can be performed in any center equipped with an extracorporeal circulation device. Under Polish conditions, mainly cardiac surgery centers with their personnel and equipment are accessible. An alternative and attractive tool can also be mobile devices that are extracorporeal techniques (ECLS/ECMO), in which, by using quick access through peripheral vessels, it is possible to stabilize the patient in shock or hypotension. The prior mentioned devices for extracorporeal perfusion techniques are more and more often used in areas of modern intensive therapy of critical states. In the Wielkopolska region, the PERT program was created in parallel with the program of universal access to extracorporeal techniques, including ECMO, as part of an organizational program "ECMO for Wielkopolska" (ECMO for Greater Poland). Such organizational cooperation gives a real chance to use a wide spectrum of applications in extracorporeal techniques in PE therapy, particularly for high risk associated with cardiogenic shock. Extracorporeal techniques with the use of ECMO in PE therapy with potential use in the treatment of PE are as follows: Veno-arterial (VA) ECMO : as a partial RV bypass in cardiogenic shock with hypotension: As part of extended cardiopulmonary resuscitation when PE is the cause of in-hospital cardiac arrest or out-hospital cardiac arrest; As a bridge to surgical embolectomy or transcatheter therapy; As RV support after surgical embolectomy in extracorporeal circulation; As a support during parenteral heparin anticoagulation. Veno-arteriovenous (VA-V) ECMO : incidentally in the treatment of shock with concomitant RV failure as a RV assist device. Veno-venous (VV) ECMO : incidentally after pulmonary embolism therapy with concomitant refractory respiratory failure with hypoxia and hypercapnia. Partial VV Angiovac system with the possibility of conversion to VA ECMO. As PERT is modeled on a philosophy of rapid response, it is crucial to constitute a clear and sound operating protocol. This protocol should accommodate PERT structure, activation pathways and operating mode. There are two basic elements of any PERT operating model. First of all, the PERT activation should be accessible via a commonly known telephone number. A dedicated on-call PERT consultant should be ready to answer a PERT activation call. The activation call may come from any healthcare provider in the region (district hospital, outpatient clinic, ambulance) networked with the PERT center in a hub-and-spoke model. The role of the PERT consultant is to collect necessary information on the patient consulted from a referring physician, including: clinical status and duration of symptoms, PE burden and hemodynamic significance, RV function and adverse outcome risk factors, comorbidities, contraindications to specific treatments like thrombolysis, surgical embolectomy or CDT. To facilitate the process of data collection, a standardized form should be in use (see the next paragraph). Depending on the PERT center institutional policies, structure and personnel resources, the PERT consultant may be an intentionally dedicated individual or any other on-call physician, who is capable of executing the PERT operating model upon activation. The second key element of the PERT operating model is cooperation between PERT specialists. The on-call PERT specialists including, at least, an interventional cardiologist and cardiac surgeon who should be ready to enter cooperation upon a PERT consultant request. There are several modes of PERT specialist mobilization, among which a staged approach seems to be the most resource efficient and practical (Fig. 1). In contrast to activation of all PERT members upfront, in the staged model the PERT consultant initially contacts one on-call PERT specialist to determine whether reperfusion therapy is needed and discuss treatment options. If a decision is not possible, another PERT specialist(s) may be asked for an opinion. After reaching a final conclusion it is communicated back to the referring physician as a PERT therapeutic recommendation. The goal should be to complete this process within 30 min from activation. If no reperfusion therapy is required at the time of consultation, the patient may continue anticoagulation treatment at the referring hospital. The referring physician should stay in touch with the PERT center in case a patient deteriorates. If, in contrast, reperfusion therapy is indicated at the site, systemic thrombolysis should primarily be considered, or if contraindications to ST are present, risk of major bleeding is high or surgical intervention is needed, the patient should be transferred to the PERT center. To support the decision-making process a therapeutic algorithm may be adapted (Fig. 2). To promote rapid and efficient course of PERT consultations, it may be useful to formulate PERT activation and decision cards. These documents should i.e. contain referral center contact details, patient demographic data, duration of symptoms, distribution of thrombi in computed tomography, clinical status and risk of death defined by contemporary algorithms (e.g. Bova score), comorbidities, risk factors of venous thromboembolism, contraindications to thrombolysis and anticipated risk of bleeding complications. Said forms may then serve as a background for the PERT decision-making process. With the advent of modern technologies, it has become available to acquire PERT activation documents in the form of mobile applications (Fig. 3). Use of mobile technologies is expected to make the process of data collection easier and more universal and to facilitate sharing information between PERT specialists during consultations. It is also desirable to record data on activations, operating modes, PERT decisions and patient follow-up in the form of a registry. A regular evaluation of accumulated data should provide insight in general PE quality measures such as mortality and morbidity, but also PERT : specific measures such as: time from activation to decision, time from decision to therapeutic anticoagulation or to reperfusion therapy, methods and effects of reperfusion treatment, PERT structure and activation modes, application of contemporary guidelines, etc. Such data may also help to improve knowledge on the role of PERT in acute PE care.
